title: حِكَايَةُ الذِّئْبِ وَالثَّعْلَبِ
part: Night 150 · The Wolf and the Fox ends / The Mouse and the Weasel / The Crow and the Cat / The Fox and the Crow begins
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 745–751 (Night 150, continuing directly from nights-149), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 150 finishes the tale of the wolf and the fox and tells three more animal fables. The wolf, trapped in the pit, pleads and flatters; the fox answers with proverbs and the parable of the serpent that begged a man to hide it from the snake-charmer and then bit him dead in payment, and calls the vineyard's owners, who stone the wolf to death while the fox recites verses over him and lives on in the vineyard in peace. Next, a weasel steals a poor man's husked sesame, and when the wife sets a watch she cleverly carries it back and lures a greedy mouse to the heap, where the wife clubs it. King Shahriyār asks for a tale of friendship that saves in time of danger, and Shahrazād tells of a crow that saves its friend the cat from a leopard by leading a shepherd's dogs to the tree. Then a fox, starving and alone, asks a crow on the mountain for friendship; the crow doubts that eater and eaten can be friends, and the fox begins the fable of the flea that fled a merchant's servants into a mouse's hole, which breaks off at dawn. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ الْخَمْسِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu al-khamsīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing the fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fiftieth night,
sentences.n: al-mūfiya, “the completing one”, names a night that ends in a ten: this one makes up the fifty after the hundred. Here the participle takes the number directly as its object, without the li- the print uses elsewhere (al-mūfiya li-al-arbaʿīn).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الذِّئْبَ لَمَّاسَمِعَ كَلَامَ الثَّعْلَبِ عَضَّ عَلَى كَفِّهِ نَدَمًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-dhiʾba lammā samiʿa kalāma al-thaʿlabi ʿaḍḍa ʿalā kaffihi nadaman
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the wolf, when he heard the speech of the fox, bit on his paw (in) regret.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the wolf heard what the fox said, he bit his paw in remorse.
sentences.n: The night opens by repeating the gesture on which the last one broke off. The print runs together al-saʿīdu anna (السعيدان) and lammā samiʿa (لماسمع); the spacing is kept. The shadda in عضّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَيَّنَ لَهُ الْكَلَامَ وَلَمْ يَجِدْبُدًّا مِنْ ذَلِكَ فَلَمْ يَنْفَعْ عِنْدَهُ شَيْأً
sentences.tr: thumma layyana lahu al-kalāma wa-lam yajid buddan min dhālika fa-lam yanfaʿ ʿindahu shayʾan
sentences.l: Then he softened for him the speech, and he did-not find escape from that; but it did-not avail with-him a thing.
sentences.i: Then he spoke softly to him, for he had no other way; but it did him no good with the fox.
sentences.n: layyana al-kalām, “to make speech soft”, to speak gently; the shadda in ليّن is the print's own. lam yajid buddan min, “he found no way out of it”: the print runs يجد and بدّا together (يجدبدا). fa-lam yanfaʿ ʿindahu shayʾan, “it availed nothing with him”: the unspoken subject is the wolf's soft talk. شيأ, with its hamza on an alif, is the print's spelling of shayʾan.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بِلِسَانٍ خَافِتٍ إِنَّكُمْ مَعَاشِرَ الثَّعَالِبِ مِنْ أَحْلَى الْقَوْمِ لِسَانًا وَأَلْطَفِهَا مِزَاحًا وَهَذَا مِنْكَ مِزَاحٌ وَلَكِنْ مَاكُلَّ وَقْتٍ يَحْسُنُ اللَّعِبُ وَالْمِزَاحُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu bi-lisānin khāfitin innakum maʿāshira al-thaʿālibi min aḥlā al-qawmi lisānan wa-alṭafihā mizāḥan wa-hādhā minka mizāḥun wa-lākin mā kulla waqtin yaḥsunu al-laʿibu wa-al-mizāḥu
sentences.l: And he said to him with a faint tongue: Truly you, (O) companies of the foxes, (are) among the sweetest of the folk in tongue and the most-graceful of-them in jesting, and this from you (is) a jest; but not (at) every time is the play and the jesting fitting.
sentences.i: And he said to him in a feeble voice, “You foxes are the sweetest-tongued of all creatures and the most graceful in jest, and this is only a jest of yours; but not every moment is the right one for play and jesting.”
sentences.n: khāfit, “low, hushed”, of a voice. maʿāshira al-thaʿālib, “you foxes as a kind”: maʿāshir, plural of maʿshar, “company, tribe”, stands in the accusative of specialisation (ikhtiṣāṣ) after innakum. alṭafihā, “the most graceful of them”: the -hā goes back to al-qawm, treated as a feminine plural. mā kulla waqtin, “not at every time”, an adverbial accusative: the print runs mā and kull together (ماكل). ḥasuna, “to be seemly, fitting”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ أَيُّهَا الْجَاهِلُ إِنَّ لِلْمِزَاحِ حَدًّا لَايُجَاوِزُهُ صَاحِبُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-thaʿlabu ayyuhā al-jāhilu inna li-al-mizāḥi ḥaddan lā yujāwizuhu ṣāḥibuhu
sentences.l: And the fox said: O ignorant-one, truly for the jesting (there is) a limit (which) its-owner does-not pass-beyond.
sentences.i: The fox said, “Fool, jesting has its bounds, and the jester does not overstep them.
sentences.n: ṣāḥibuhu, “its owner”, the one who jests. The print runs lā and the verb together (لايجاوزه).

sentences.t: فَلَاتَظُنَّ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُمَكِّنُكَ مِنِّي بَعْدَ أَنْ أَنْقَذَنِي مِنْ يَدَيْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lā taẓunna anna allāha yumakkinuka minnī baʿda an anqadhanī min yadayka
sentences.l: So do-not think that God will-give-you-mastery over-me, after He has-rescued-me from your-two-hands.
sentences.i: So do not imagine that God will put me in your power, after He has saved me from your clutches.”
sentences.n: makkanahu min, “to give someone mastery over”. lā taẓunna, a prohibition: in the jussive a doubled verb may keep its doubling and take a fatḥa (taẓunna, beside taẓnun). The shaddas in فلاتظنّ, يمكّنك and منّي are the print's own; fa-lā is run together with the verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الذِّئْبُ إِنَّكَ لَجَدِيرٌأَنْ تَرْغَبَ فِي خَلَاصِي لِمَا بَيْنَنَا مِنْ سَابِقِ الْمُوَاخَاةِ وَالصُّحْبَةِ وَإِنْ خَلَّصْتَنِي لَابُدَّأَنْ أُحْسِنَ مُكَافَأَتَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-dhiʾbu innaka la-jadīrun an targhaba fī khalāṣī li-mā baynanā min sābiqi al-muwākhāti wa-al-ṣuḥbati wa-in khallaṣtanī lā budda an uḥsina mukāfaʾataka
sentences.l: And the wolf said to him: Truly you (are) indeed worthy that you-should-desire my-deliverance, for what (is) between-us of former brotherhood and the companionship; and if you-deliver-me, there-is-no escape (but) that I make-good your-reward.
sentences.i: The wolf said to him, “You surely ought to want me freed, for the sake of the brotherhood and companionship there has long been between us; and if you get me out, I am bound to reward you handsomely.”
sentences.n: The print runs together la-jadīrun an (لجديران) and lā budda an (لابدان). jadīr an, “fit, deserving to”. muwākhāh, “brotherhood, sworn friendship”, is written with w for the Classical muʾākhāh: the hamza has softened into a glide, a Middle Arabic form. aḥsana mukāfaʾatahu, “to reward someone well”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ إِنَّ الْحُكَمَاءَ قَالُوا لَاتُوَاخِ الْجَاهِلَ الْفَاجِرَ فَإِنَّهُ يَشِينُكَ وَلَايَزِينُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-thaʿlabu inna al-ḥukamāʾa qālū lā tuwākhi al-jāhila al-fājira fa-innahu yashīnuka wa-lā yazīnuka
sentences.l: And the fox said: Truly the wise-ones have-said: Do-not take-as-brother the ignorant, the wicked, for he disgraces-you and does-not adorn-you;
sentences.i: The fox said, “The wise have said: Make no brother of a wicked fool, for he will shame you and never grace you;
sentences.n: lā tuwākhi, the prohibition of wākhā (Classical ākhā), “to take as a brother”: the final long vowel drops in the jussive. yashīnuka / yazīnuka, “he disgraces you / he adorns you”, a rhyming pair. The print runs lā and the verb together in لاتواخ and لايزينك.

sentences.t: وَلَاتُوَاخِ الْكَذَّابَ فَإِنَّهُ إِنْ بَدَامِنْكَ خَيْرٌ أَخْفَاهُ وَإِنْ بَدَامِنْكَ شَرٌّأَفْشَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lā tuwākhi al-kadhdhāba fa-innahu in badā minka khayrun akhfāhu wa-in badā minka sharrun afshāhu
sentences.l: and do-not take-as-brother the liar, for he, if good shows from-you, hides-it, and if evil shows from-you, spreads-it-abroad.
sentences.i: and make no brother of a liar, for if any good shows in you he hides it, and if any evil shows he noises it abroad.
sentences.n: badā, “to appear, show itself”. akhfāhu / afshāhu, “he hides it / he spreads it”, rhyme. The print runs badā minka together twice (بدامنك), and sharrun with afshāhu (شرافشاه).

sentences.t: وَقَالَتِ الْحُكَمَاءُ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ حِيلَةٌ إِلَّا الْمَوْتَ وَيُصْلَحُ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ إِلَّافَسَادَ الْجَوْهَرِ وَقَدْيُدْفَعُ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ إِلَّا الْقَدَرَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālati al-ḥukamāʾu li-kulli shayʾin ḥīlatun illā al-mawta wa-yuṣlaḥu kullu shayʾin illā fasāda al-jawhari wa-qad yudfaʿu kullu shayʾin illā al-qadara
sentences.l: And the wise-ones have-said: For every thing (there is) a device except the death; and every thing is-mended except the corruption of the substance; and every thing may be-warded-off except the decree.
sentences.i: The wise have also said: There is a remedy for everything but death; everything can be mended but a flaw in the very substance; and everything may be warded off but fate.
sentences.n: ḥīla, “a stratagem, a way out”. jawhar, “substance, essence; a jewel”: what is rotten in its nature cannot be put right. The print sets illā fasāda as one word, الافساد, which looks like al-ifsād, “corrupting”; the sense requires illā, “except”, and the word is read so. qad with the imperfect, “may, at times”, is run into its verb (وقديدفع). qadar, “fate, what God has decreed”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مِنْ جِهَةِ الْمُكَافَأَةِ الَّتِي زَعَمْتَ أَنِّي أَسْتَحِقُّهَا مِنْكَ فَإِنِّي شَبَّهْتُكَ فِي مُكَافَأَتِكَ بِالْحَيَّةِ الْهَارِبَةِ مِنَ الْحَاوِي إِذْرَآهَا رَجُلٌ وَهِيَ مَرْعُوبَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā min jihati al-mukāfaʾati allatī zaʿamta annī astaḥiqquhā minka fa-innī shabbahtuka fī mukāfaʾatika bi-al-ḥayyati al-hāribati mina al-ḥāwī idh raʾāhā rajulun wa-hiya marʿūbatun
sentences.l: And as for the side of the reward which you-claimed that I deserve-it from-you, then I have-likened-you in your-rewarding to the serpent, the fleeing-one from the snake-charmer, when a man saw-her, and she (was) terrified.
sentences.i: As for the reward you claim I have earned from you, in the way you repay I liken you to the serpent fleeing from the snake-charmer. A man saw her in her terror
sentences.n: zaʿama, “to claim, allege”, often of something untrue. ḥāwī, “snake-charmer”, one who catches and handles snakes. ḥayya is feminine, and the serpent is “she” throughout. The print runs idh and raʾāhā together (اذرآها); the shadda in شبّهتك is its own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَا شَأْنُكِ أَيَّتُهَا الْحَيَّةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā shaʾnuki ayyatuhā al-ḥayyatu
sentences.l: and said to her: What (is) your-affair, O serpent?
sentences.i: and said to her, ‘What is the matter with you, serpent?’
sentences.n: mā shaʾnuki, “what is your affair?”, what is wrong with you; the print writes shaʾn without its hamza (شانك). ayyatuhā is the feminine of ayyuhā, “O”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ هَرَبْتُ مِنَ الْحَاوِي فَإِنَّهُ يَطْلُبُنِي وَلَئِنْ أَنْجَيْتَنِي مِنْهُ وَأَخْفَيْتَنِي عِنْدَكَ لَأُحْسِنَنَّ مُكَافَأَتَكَ وَأَصْنَعُ مَعَكَ كُلَّ جَمِيلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat harabtu mina al-ḥāwī fa-innahu yaṭlubunī wa-la-in anjaytanī minhu wa-akhfaytanī ʿindaka la-uḥsinanna mukāfaʾataka wa-aṣnaʿu maʿaka kulla jamīlin
sentences.l: And she said: I-have-fled from the snake-charmer, for he is-seeking-me; and if you-save-me from-him and hide-me with-you, I-will-surely make-good your-reward and do with-you every fair-thing.
sentences.i: ‘I am fleeing from the snake-charmer,’ she answered, ‘for he is hunting me. If you save me from him and hide me with you, I will reward you richly and do you every kindness.’
sentences.n: la-in …, la-uḥsinanna, “if indeed …, I shall surely …”: the la- on in announces an oath-like promise, and the energetic -anna on the verb seals it; the second verb, aṣnaʿu, goes on without it. ṣanaʿa maʿahu jamīlan, “to do someone a good turn”.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهَا اغْتِنَامًا لِلْأَجْرِ وَطَمَعًا فِى الْمُكَافَأَةِ فَأَدْخَلَهَا فِي جَيْبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahā ightināman li-al-ajri wa-ṭamaʿan fī al-mukāfaʾati fa-adkhalahā fī jaybihi
sentences.l: And he took-her, seizing-the-chance for the (heavenly) wage and in-greed for the reward, and put-her into his breast-pocket.
sentences.i: So he took her up, glad of the chance to earn merit with God and greedy for the reward, and slipped her into the breast of his robe.
sentences.n: ightinām, “seizing as booty, making the most of”. ajr, “wage”, here the reward God gives for a good deed, set beside the serpent's promised mukāfaʾa. jayb is the opening at the breast of a garment, used as a pocket. The two accusatives, ightināman and ṭamaʿan, give his motives.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَاتَ الْحَاوِي وَمَضَى إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ وَزَالَ عَنِ الْحَيَّةِ مَاكَانَتْ تَخَافُهُ قَالَ لَهَا الرَّجُلُ أَيْنَ الْمُكَافَأَةُ فَقَدْ أَنْجَيْتُكِ مِمَّاتَخَافِينَ وَتَحْذَرِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā fāta al-ḥāwī wa-maḍā ilā ḥāli sabīlihi wa-zāla ʿani al-ḥayyati mā kānat takhāfuhu qāla lahā al-rajulu ayna al-mukāfaʾatu fa-qad anjaytuki mimmā takhāfīna wa-taḥdharīna
sentences.l: And when the snake-charmer had-passed-by and gone-on to the state of his-way, and there-had-left the serpent what she-was fearing, the man said to-her: Where (is) the reward? For I-have-saved-you from-what you-fear and beware-of.
sentences.i: When the snake-charmer had gone by and passed on his way, and the serpent's fear had left her, the man said to her, ‘Where is my reward? I have saved you from all you feared and dreaded.’
sentences.n: The print has تخانه, a misprint for تخافه, corrected here. fāta, “to go past”. maḍā ilā ḥāli sabīlihi, “he went off about his business”. The print runs together mā kānat (ماكانت) and mimmā takhāfīna (مماتخافين).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْحَيَّةُ أَخْبِرْنِي فِي أَيِّ عُضْوٍ وَفِي أَيِّ مَوْضِعٍ أَنْهَشُكَ فَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ أَنَّنَا لَانَتَجَاوَزُ هَذِهِ الْمُكَافَأَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ḥayyatu akhbirnī fī ayyi ʿuḍwin wa-fī ayyi mawḍiʿin anhashuka fa-qad ʿalimta annanā lā natajāwazu hādhihi al-mukāfaʾata
sentences.l: And the serpent said to-him: Tell-me in which limb and in which place I-shall-bite-you, for you-have-known that we do-not go-beyond this reward.
sentences.i: The serpent said to him, ‘Tell me in which limb, and in which spot, I am to bite you; for you know well that we never pay any other reward than this.’
sentences.n: nahasha, “to bite, strike”, of a snake. annanā, “we”: the serpent speaks for all her kind. The print runs lā and the verb together (لانتجاوز).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَهَشَتْهُ نَهْشَةً مَاتَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma nahashathu nahshatan māta minhā
sentences.l: Then she-bit-him a bite (that) he-died from-it.
sentences.i: Then she struck him, and he died of the bite.
sentences.n: nahshatan, the verb's own noun as its object, “she bit him a bite”.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ أَيُّهَا الْأَحْمَقُ شَبَّهْتُكَ بِتِلْكَ الْحَيَّةِ مَعَ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلِ
sentences.tr: wa-anta ayyuhā al-aḥmaqu shabbahtuka bi-tilka al-ḥayyati maʿa dhālika al-rajuli
sentences.l: And you, O fool, I-have-likened-you to that serpent with that man.
sentences.i: And you, fool, I have likened to that serpent and the way she dealt with that man.
sentences.n: wa-anta … shabbahtuka, the person set first and taken up again by the pronoun: “as for you, I liken you”.

sentences.t: أَمَا سَمِعْتَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: a-mā samiʿta qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: Have-you not heard the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: Have you not heard the poet's words:

sentences.t:
لَا تَأْمَنَنَّ فَتًى اَسْكَنْتَ مُهْجَتَهُ * غَيْظًا وَتَحْسَبُ اَنَّ الْغَيْظَ قَدْ زَالَا
اِنَّ الْاَفَاعِيْ وَاِنْ لَانَتْ مَلَامِسُهَا * تُبْدِى الْعِطَافَا وَتُخْفِى السَّمَّ قَتَّالَا
sentences.tr:
lā taʾmananna fatan askanta muhjatahu * ghayẓan wa-taḥsabu anna al-ghayẓa qad zālā
inna al-afāʿī wa-in lānat malāmisuhā * tubdī al-ʿiṭāfā wa-tukhfī al-samma qattālā
sentences.l:
Do-not trust-indeed a youth whose heart-blood you-have-lodged (with) rage, while you-reckon that the rage has gone-away;
truly the vipers, even-if their touching-places be-soft, show the flanks and hide the poison, killing.
sentences.i:
Never trust a man whose heart you have filled with rage, thinking that his rage has passed;
vipers, however soft they are to the touch, show you their supple sides and hide their deadly venom.”
sentences.n: lā taʾmananna, “never trust”, with the energetic -anna. muhja, “heart's blood, life”: askanta muhjatahu ghayẓan, “you lodged rage in his heart”. malāmis, “the places one touches”, the skin. afāʿī, plural of afʿā, “viper”; the print gives its final yāʾ a sukūn (الْاَفَاعِيْ), its way of marking a long ī. ʿiṭāf here is taken as the plural of ʿiṭf, “side, flank”: the long final ā of الْعِطَافَا is unusual in mid-line and the reading is not certain; ʿiṭāf can also mean “a cloak”, but the soft sides they show suit the soft touch of the first half. qattālan, “deadly”, describes the poison. The verse hamza is pointed as a bare alif with its vowel (اَسْكَنْتَ, اَنَّ), as the print does.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الذِّئْبُ أَيُّهَا الْفَصِيحُ صَاحِبُ الْوَجْهِ الْمَلِيحِ لَا تَجْهَلْ حَالِي وَخَوْفَ النَّاسِ مِنِّي وَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ أَنِّي أَهْجُمُ عَلَى الْحُصُونِ وَأَقْلَعُ الْكُرُومَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-dhiʾbu ayyuhā al-faṣīḥu ṣāḥibu al-wajhi al-malīḥi lā tajhal ḥālī wa-khawfa al-nāsi minnī wa-qad ʿalimta annī ahjumu ʿalā al-ḥuṣūni wa-aqlaʿu al-kurūma
sentences.l: And the wolf said to him: O eloquent-one, owner of the comely face, do-not be-ignorant-of my-state and the fear of the people of-me; and you-have-known that I fall upon the fortresses and uproot the vines.
sentences.i: The wolf said to him, “O eloquent one with the handsome face, do not forget who I am and how men fear me: you know that I storm fortresses and tear up vineyards.
sentences.n: Rhyme: faṣīḥ / malīḥ, the wolf turning to flattery. The boast is empty: kurūm, plural of karm, “vineyards”, are the very thing he lies trapped in.

sentences.t: فَافْعَلْ مَا أَمَرْتُكَ بِهِ وَقُمْ بِي قِيَامَ الْعَبْدِ بِسَيِّدِةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ifʿal mā amartuka bihi wa-qum bī qiyāma al-ʿabdi bi-sayyidihi
sentences.l: So do what I-have-ordered-you with-it, and attend on-me (with) the attending of the slave on his-master.
sentences.i: So do as I bid you, and serve me as a slave serves his master.”
sentences.n: amarahu bi-, “to order someone to (do) something”. qāma bi-, “to see to, look after”: qiyāma al-ʿabdi bi-sayyidihi, “as a slave looks after his master”. The print writes بسيّدة, with tāʾ marbūṭa where the pronoun -hi, “his”, is meant: the edition's spelling, the reverse of its common ه for ة. It is kept and read bi-sayyidihi. The shadda is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الثَّعْلَبُ أَيُّهَا الْأَحْمَقُ الْجَاهِلُ الْمُحَاوِلُ بِالْبَاطِلِ إِنِّي تَعَجَّبْتُ مِنْ حُمْقِكَ وَصَلَابَةِ وَجْهِكَ فِيمَا تَأْمُرُنِي بِهِ مِنْ خِدْمَتِكَ وَالْقِيَامِ بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ حَتَّى كَأَنَّنِي عَبْدُكَ اشْتَرَيْتَنِي بِمَالِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-thaʿlabu ayyuhā al-aḥmaqu al-jāhilu al-muḥāwilu bi-al-bāṭili innī taʿajjabtu min ḥumqika wa-ṣalābati wajhika fīmā taʾmurunī bihi min khidmatika wa-al-qiyāmi bayna yadayka ḥattā kaʾannanī ʿabduka ishtaraytanī bi-mālika
sentences.l: And the fox said to him: O fool, the ignorant, the one-striving after the vain, truly I have-marvelled at your-folly and the hardness of your-face, in what you-order-me with-it of serving-you and the standing between your-two-hands, until as-if I (were) your-slave (whom) you-bought-me with your-wealth.
sentences.i: The fox said to him, “You ignorant fool, grasping at nothing! I marvel at your folly and your brazen face, ordering me to serve you and wait on you as though I were a slave you had bought with your money.
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-jāhil / al-muḥāwil / bi-al-bāṭil. ḥāwala, “to attempt, strive after”: al-muḥāwil bi-al-bāṭil, “who reaches for what is vain”. ṣalābat al-wajh, “hardness of face”, effrontery. al-qiyām bayna yadayhi, “standing before him”, waiting on him. ʿabduka ishtaraytanī, “your slave you bought me”: the -nī takes up the slave in the clause that describes him. The shadda in تعجّبت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَسَوْفَ تَرَى مَا يَحُلُّ بِكَ مِنْ شَدْخِ رَأْسِكَ بِالْحِجَارَةِ وَكَسْرِ أَنْيَابِكَ الْغَدَّارَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-sawfa tarā mā yaḥullu bika min shadkhi raʾsika bi-al-ḥijārati wa-kasri anyābika al-ghaddārati
sentences.l: So you-will-see what comes-down on-you, of the crushing of your-head with the stones and the breaking of your-fangs, the treacherous.
sentences.i: You will soon see what is coming to you: your head smashed with stones and your treacherous fangs broken.”
sentences.n: ḥalla bi-, “to come down upon, befall”. shadkh, “crushing” something hollow, as a skull. Rhyme: ḥijāra / ghaddāra.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَقَفَ الثَّعْلَبُ فَوْقَ تَلٍّ يُشْرِفُ عَلَى الْكَرْمِ فَصَاحَ الثَّعْلَبُ عَلَى أَهْلِ الْكَرْمِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَصِيحُ حَتَّى نَبَّهَهُمْ وَبَصُرُوابِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma waqafa al-thaʿlabu fawqa tallin yushrifu ʿalā al-karmi fa-ṣāḥa al-thaʿlabu ʿalā ahli al-karmi wa-lam yazal yaṣīḥu ḥattā nabbahahum wa-baṣurū bihi
sentences.l: Then the fox stood on-top-of a hillock (that) overlooks the vineyard, and the fox cried-out at the people of the vineyard, and he did-not cease crying until he-roused-them and they-caught-sight of-him.
sentences.i: Then the fox took his stand on a hillock overlooking the vineyard and shouted at the vineyard folk, and went on shouting until he had roused them and they caught sight of him.
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, “to overlook, look down on”. baṣura bi-, “to catch sight of”: the print runs the verb and bihi together (وبصروابه). The shaddas in تلّ and نبّههم are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلُوا عَلَيْهِ بِجَمْعِهِمْ مُسْرِعِينَ فَثَبَتَ لَهُمُ الثَّعْلَبُ حَتَّى قَرُبُوا مِنْهُ وَمِنَ الْحَفِيرَةِ الَّتِي فِيهَا الذِّئْبُ ثُمَّ وَلَّى الثَّعْلَبُ هَارِبًا
sentences.tr: wa-aqbalū ʿalayhi bi-jamʿihim musriʿīna fa-thabata lahumu al-thaʿlabu ḥattā qarubū minhu wa-mina al-ḥafīrati allatī fīhā al-dhiʾbu thumma wallā al-thaʿlabu hāriban
sentences.l: And they-came-on toward-him with their-whole-band, hurrying; and the fox stood-firm for-them until they-drew-near to-him and to the pit in-which (was) the wolf; then the fox turned-away, fleeing.
sentences.i: They came at him all together, at a run, and the fox held his ground until they were close to him and to the pit where the wolf was; then he turned and fled.
sentences.n: bi-jamʿihim, “with their whole company”, in a body. ḥafīra, “a dug pit”, the wolf's trap. wallā hāriban, “he turned his back in flight”.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ أَصْحَابُ الْكَرْمِ فِى الْحَفِيرَةِ فَرَأَوُا الذِّئْبَ فِيهَا فَمَالُوا عَلَيْهِ بِالْحِجَارَةِ الثِّقَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara aṣḥābu al-karmi fī al-ḥafīrati fa-raʾawu al-dhiʾba fīhā fa-mālū ʿalayhi bi-al-ḥijārati al-thiqāli
sentences.l: And the owners of the vineyard looked into the pit and saw the wolf in-it, and they turned upon-him with the stones, the heavy.
sentences.i: The vineyard men looked into the pit and saw the wolf in it, and they set upon him with heavy stones.
sentences.n: aṣḥāb al-karm, “the owners of the vineyard”, the men who keep it. māla ʿalā, “to turn upon, fall on”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا يَضْرِبُونَهُ بِالْحِجَارَةِ وَالْخَشَبِ وَيَطْعَنُونَهُ بِأَسِنَّةِ الرِّمَاحِ حَتَّى قَتَلُوهُ وَانْصَرَفُوا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū yaḍribūnahu bi-al-ḥijārati wa-al-khashabi wa-yaṭʿanūnahu bi-asinnati al-rimāḥi ḥattā qatalūhu wa-inṣarafū
sentences.l: And they did-not cease beating-him with the stones and the wood and piercing-him with the heads of the spears, until they-killed-him and went-away.
sentences.i: They went on beating him with stones and sticks and stabbing him with spear-points until they had killed him; then they went off.
sentences.n: khashab, “wood”, here cudgels. asinna, plural of sinān, “spearhead”.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَ الثَّعْلَبُ إِلَى تِلْكَ الْحُفْرَةِ وَوَقَفَ عَلَى مَقْتَلِ الذِّئْبِ فَرَأٰهُ مَيِّتًا فَحَرَّكَ رَأْسَهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْفَرَحَاتِ وَجَعَلَ يُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿa al-thaʿlabu ilā tilka al-ḥufrati wa-waqafa ʿalā maqtali al-dhiʾbi fa-raʾāhu mayyitan fa-ḥarraka raʾsahu min shiddati al-faraḥāti wa-jaʿala yunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And the fox returned to that pit, and stood over the place-of-slaying of the wolf, and saw-him dead; and he moved his-head from the intensity of the joys, and began reciting these verses:
sentences.i: The fox came back to the pit and stood over the spot where the wolf had been killed, and saw him dead. He wagged his head in the fullness of his delight and began to recite these verses:
sentences.n: The print writes فرأه for fa-raʾāhu, without the long ā usually written رآه; the dagger alif here supplies it. maqtal, “the place of slaying”. al-faraḥāt is an odd plural, “joys”, where al-faraḥ, “joy”, is expected; the print's form is kept. ḥarraka raʾsahu, “he shook his head”, here in glee. jaʿala with an imperfect, “he set about, began to”; anshada, “to recite verse”.

sentences.t:
اَوْدَى الزَّمَانُ بِنَفْسِ الذِّئْبِ فَاخْتَطَفَتْ * بُعْدًا وَسُحْقًا لَهَا مِنْ مُهْجَةٍ تَلَفَتْ
فَكَمْ سَعَيْتَ اَيَا سَرْحَانُ فِيْ تَلَفِيْ * فَالْيَوْمَ حَلَّتْ بِكَ الْاَفَاتُ وَالْتَصَقَتْ
وَقَعْتَ فِيْ حُفْرَةٍ مَا حَلَّهَا اَحَدٌ * اِلَّا وَفِيهَا رِيَاحُ الْمَوْتِ قَدْ عَصَفَتْ
sentences.tr:
awdā al-zamānu bi-nafsi al-dhiʾbi fa-ikhtaṭafat * buʿdan wa-suḥqan lahā min muhjatin talafat
fa-kam saʿayta ayā sarḥānu fī talafī * fa-al-yawma ḥallat bika al-āfātu wa-iltaṣaqat
waqaʿta fī ḥufratin mā ḥallahā aḥadun * illā wa-fīhā riyāḥu al-mawti qad ʿaṣafat
sentences.l:
Time has-made-away with the soul of the wolf, and it was-snatched-off: far-off and away with-it, of a heart's-blood (that) perished!
How-much you-strove, O wolf, in my-ruin! So today the calamities have-come-down on-you and stuck-fast.
You-fell into a pit (which) not anyone came-down-into-it but in-it the winds of the death had stormed.
sentences.i:
Time has made an end of the wolf's life, and it was snatched away: good riddance to a soul now perished!
How long you laboured, wolf, for my undoing; today calamities have come down on you and cling fast.
You fell into a pit that no one ever entered but the gales of death blew hard within.
sentences.n: awdā bi-, “to destroy, make away with”. ikhtaṭafat is pointed as active, “it snatched”, where the sense wants “it was snatched”; the line may intend the passive, and the rendering follows the sense. buʿdan wa-suḥqan lahā, “far away and to perdition with it!”, a curse in the accusative (compare Qurʾān 67:11, fa-suḥqan). talafat, “perished”: Classical has talifa; the print's form is kept. sarḥān, “wolf”, a poetic name; ayā, “O”. al-āfāt, “calamities”, is printed without its madda (الْاَفَاتُ). mā … illā wa-, “no one … but that …”: whoever came down into that pit met death there.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الثَّعْلَبَ أَقَامَ بِالْكَرْمِ وَحْدَهُ مُطْمَئِنًّا لَا يَخَافُ ضَرَرًا إِلَى أَنْ أَتَاهُ الْمَوْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-thaʿlaba aqāma bi-al-karmi waḥdahu muṭmaʾinnan lā yakhāfu ḍararan ilā an atāhu al-mawtu
sentences.l: Then truly the fox stayed in the vineyard alone, at-rest, not fearing harm, until (that) the death came-to-him.
sentences.i: And from then on the fox lived in the vineyard by himself, at peace and fearing no harm, until death came to him.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then, (indeed)”, the narrator's formula for moving a story on. muṭmaʾinn, “at rest, secure”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ حَدِيثِ الذِّئْبِ وَالثَّعْلَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā mā kāna min ḥadīthi al-dhiʾbi wa-al-thaʿlabi
sentences.l: And this (is) what was of the story of the wolf and the fox.
sentences.i: And that is the story of the wolf and the fox.
sentences.n: The closing formula of a tale, “this is what there was of the story of …”. The print runs mā kāna together (ماكان).

sentences.t: وَمِمَّا يُحْكَى أَنَّ فَأْرَةً وَبِنْتَ عِرْسٍ كَانَا يَنْزِلَانِ مَنْزِلًا لِدِهْقَانٍ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الدِّهْقَانُ فَقِيرًا
sentences.tr: wa-mimmā yuḥkā anna faʾratan wa-binta ʿirsin kānā yanzilāni manzilan li-dihqānin wa-kāna dhālika al-dihqānu faqīran
sentences.l: And of-what is-told: that a mouse and a daughter-of-ʿirs (weasel) were-two lodging (in) a lodging belonging-to a dihqān, and that dihqān was poor.
sentences.i: And among the things that are told is this: a mouse and a weasel lodged together in the house of a peasant, and that peasant was poor.
sentences.n: A new fable begins. bint ʿirs, literally “daughter of a bridegroom”, is the weasel. kānā yanzilāni, “the two were lodging”, uses the masculine dual for two female animals; Classical Arabic would say kānatā tanzilāni. This is Middle Arabic, where the masculine dual commonly serves for both genders. dihqān, a Persian loanword, first meant a landed village chief; here it is simply a countryman, a small farmer.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ مَرِضَ بَعْضُ أَصْدِقَائِهِ فَوَصَفَ لَهُ الطَّبِيبُ السِّمْسِمَ الْمَقْشُورَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad mariḍa baʿḍu aṣdiqāʾihi fa-waṣafa lahu al-ṭabību al-simsima al-maqshūra
sentences.l: And one of his friends had fallen-sick, and the physician prescribed for-him the sesame, the husked.
sentences.i: Now one of his friends had fallen ill, and the physician prescribed husked sesame for him.
sentences.n: waṣafa lahu, literally “described for him”, is the regular word for a doctor prescribing a remedy.

sentences.t: فَطَلَبَ مِنْ بَعْضِ أَصْحَابِهِ سِمْسِمًا يُقَشِّرُهُ لِمَرَضٍ أَصَابَهُ فَأَعْطَا قَدْرًا مِنَ السِّمْسِمِ لِذَلِكَ الدِّهْقَانِ الْفَقِيرِ لِيُقَشِّرَهُ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaba min baʿḍi aṣḥābihi simsiman yuqashshiruhu li-maraḍin aṣābahu fa-aʿṭā qadran mina al-simsimi li-dhālika al-dihqāni al-faqīri li-yuqashshirahu lahu
sentences.l: So he asked from some-one of his companions (for) sesame that he-would-husk-it, for a sickness that had-struck-him; and he gave a quantity of the sesame to that dihqān, the poor-one, so-that he-might-husk-it for-him.
sentences.i: So he asked one of his companions to husk some sesame for him, because of the illness that had struck him; and he gave a measure of sesame to that poor peasant to husk for him.
sentences.n: The print spells aʿṭā, “he gave”, with a final alif, فاعطا, where Classical spelling has ى; the spelling is kept. Who gives the sesame is left loose: the sick man, through his friend, passes it to the poor peasant to be husked.

sentences.t: فَأَتَى بِهِ إِلَى زَوْجَتِهِ وَأَمَرَهَا بِإِصْلَاحِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-atā bihi ilā zawjatihi wa-amarahā bi-iṣlāḥihi
sentences.l: And he came with-it to his wife and ordered-her with its-preparing.
sentences.i: He brought it to his wife and told her to prepare it.
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to come with, bring”: the verb chooses the preposition. amara bi-, “to order (someone) to do”, likewise takes bi- before the thing ordered. iṣlāḥ, “setting right, preparing”.

sentences.t: فَبَلَّتْهُ وَنَشَرَتْهُ وَجَفَّفَتْهُ وَأَصْلَحَتْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ballathu wa-nasharathu wa-jaffafathu wa-aṣlaḥathu
sentences.l: And she moistened-it, and spread-it-out, and dried-it, and prepared-it.
sentences.i: She wetted it, spread it out, dried it, and dressed it.
sentences.n: The print has خففته, a misprint for جففته, corrected here: jaffafathu, “she dried it”, as the sesame is called mujaffaf, “dried”, a few lines on. The shadda in بلّته is the print's own: ballathu, “she moistened it”, the soaking that loosens sesame husks.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَايَنَتْ بِنْتُ عِرْسٍ السِّمْسِمَ أَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَنْقُلُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ السِّمْسِمِ إِلَى جُحْرِهَا طُولَ يَوْمِهَا حَتَّى نَقَلَتْ أَكْثَرَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿāyanat bintu ʿirsin al-simsima atat ilayhi wa-lam tazal tanqulu min dhālika al-simsimi ilā juḥrihā ṭūla yawmihā ḥattā naqalat aktharahu
sentences.l: And when the weasel set-eyes-on the sesame, she came to-it, and did-not cease carrying from that sesame to her hole the length of her day, until she had-carried most-of-it.
sentences.i: When the weasel caught sight of the sesame, she went to it, and all day long she kept carrying it off to her hole, until she had taken most of it.
sentences.n: ʿāyana, “to see with one's own eyes”, from ʿayn, “eye”. lam tazal, “she did not cease”, with a present verb, “she kept on doing”. juḥr, “a burrow, an animal's hole”.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ فَرَأَتْ نُقْصَانَ السِّمْسِمِ وَاضِحًا فَوَقَفَتْ تَتَعَجَّبُ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾati al-marʾatu fa-raʾat nuqṣāna al-simsimi wāḍiḥan fa-waqafat tataʿajjabu
sentences.l: And the woman came and saw the decrease of the sesame (to be) plain, and she stood wondering.
sentences.i: Then the woman came and saw plainly that the sesame had gone down, and she stood there in wonder.
sentences.n: wāḍiḥan, “plain, evident”, a circumstantial accusative describing the loss as she saw it.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَتْ تَرْصُدُ مَنْ يَأْتِي إِلَيْهِ حَتَّى تَعْلَمَ سَبَبَ نُقْصَانِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasat tarṣudu man yaʾtī ilayhi ḥattā taʿlama sababa nuqṣānihi
sentences.l: And she sat lying-in-wait-for whoever comes to-it, so-that she might-know the cause of its decrease.
sentences.i: So she sat down to watch for whoever came to it, so as to learn why it was going down.
sentences.n: raṣada, “to watch for, lie in wait for”, recurs through the fable, with mirṣād, “a lookout, an ambush”, in a moment.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتْ بِنْتُ عِرْسٍ لِتَنْقُلَ مِنْهُ عَلَى عَادَتِهَا فَرَأَتِ الْمَرْأَةَ جَالِسَةً فَعَلِمَتْ أَنَّهَا تَرْصُدُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat bintu ʿirsin li-tanqula minhu ʿalā ʿādatihā fa-raʾati al-marʾata jālisatan fa-ʿalimat annahā tarṣuduhā
sentences.l: And the weasel came-down to carry from-it according-to her custom, and she saw the woman sitting, and knew that she was-lying-in-wait-for-her.
sentences.i: The weasel came down to carry off some more as usual, saw the woman sitting there, and knew that she was watching for her.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا إِنَّ لِهَذَا الْفِعْلِ عَوَاقِبَ ذَمِيمَةً وَإِنِّي أَخْشَي مِنْ تِلْكَ الْمَرْأَةِ أَنْ تَكُونَ لِي بِالْمِرْصَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat fī nafsihā inna li-hādhā al-fiʿli ʿawāqiba dhamīmatan wa-innī akhshā min tilka al-marʾati an takūna lī bi-al-mirṣādi
sentences.l: And she said in her-self: Indeed to this deed (belong) consequences blameworthy, and indeed-I fear from that woman that she be for-me at-the-lookout.
sentences.i: She said to herself, “This business will have ugly consequences, and I fear that woman is lying in wait for me.
sentences.n: The print spells akhshā, “I fear”, with ي where Classical spelling has ى, اخشي; the spelling is kept. kāna lahu bi-al-mirṣād, “to be in ambush for someone”, after Qurʾān 89:14, inna rabbaka la-bi-al-mirṣād, “your Lord is ever on the watch”.

sentences.t: وَمَنْ لَمْ يَنْظُرْ فِى الْعَوَاقِبِ مَا الدَّهْرُ لَهُ بِصَاحِبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-man lam yanẓur fī al-ʿawāqibi mā al-dahru lahu bi-ṣāḥibin
sentences.l: And whoever has-not looked into the consequences, not (is) time for-him a-companion.
sentences.i: Whoever does not look to the consequences will find fortune no friend of his.
sentences.n: A proverb. al-dahr, “time”, the long run of days that brings fortune and ruin. mā … bi-ṣāḥibin: after the negative mā the predicate may take bi-, which only strengthens the denial, “no friend at all”.

sentences.t: وَلَا بُدَّ لِي أَنْ أَعْمَلَ عَمَلًا حَسَنًا أُظْهِرُ بِهِ بَرَاءَتِي وَأَغْسِلُ بِهِ جَمِيعَ مَا عَمِلْتُهُ مِنَ الْقَبِيحِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā budda lī an aʿmala ʿamalan ḥasanan uẓhiru bihi barāʾatī wa-aghsilu bihi jamīʿa mā ʿamiltuhu mina al-qabīḥi
sentences.l: And there-is-no escape for-me (but) that I do a deed fair, I-show by-it my-innocence and I-wash by-it all that I-have-done of the foul.
sentences.i: I must do some good deed to show my innocence and wash away by it all the wrong I have done.”
sentences.n: lā budda lī an, “I must”; the shadda in بدّ is the print's own. barāʾa, “innocence, being clear of blame”. mina al-qabīḥ, “of the ugly”: min here says what kind of thing she had done.

sentences.t: فَجَعَلَتْ تَنْقُلُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ السِّمْسِمِ الَّذِي فِي بَيْتِهَا وَتُخْرِجُهُ وَتَجِيءُ بِهِ وَتَضَعُهُ عَلَى السِّمْسِمِ
sentences.tr: fa-jaʿalat tanqulu min dhālika al-simsimi alladhī fī baytihā wa-tukhrijuhu wa-tajīʾu bihi wa-taḍaʿuhu ʿalā al-simsimi
sentences.l: And she began carrying from that sesame which (was) in her house, and bringing-it-out, and coming with-it, and putting-it on the sesame.
sentences.i: So she began to carry back the sesame that was in her hole: she brought it out, carried it over, and put it back on the pile.
sentences.n: jaʿala with a present verb, “to begin doing”. jāʾa bi-, “to come with, bring”.

sentences.t: فَوَافَتْهَا الْمَرْأَةُ وَرَأَتْهَا وَهِيَ تَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-wāfathā al-marʾatu wa-raʾathā wa-hiya tafʿalu dhālika
sentences.l: And the woman came-upon-her and saw-her while she (was) doing that.
sentences.i: The woman came upon her and saw her doing it.
sentences.n: wāfā, “to come upon, arrive at the moment of”. wa-hiya tafʿalu, a circumstantial clause, “while she was doing”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا مَاهَذِهِ سَبَبُ نَقْصِهِ لِأَنَّهَا تَأْتِي بِهِ مِنْ جُحْرِ الَّذِي اخْتَلَسَهُ وَتَضَعُهُ عَلَى بَعْضِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat fī nafsihā mā hādhihi sababu naqṣihi li-annahā taʾtī bihi min juḥri alladhī ikhtalasahu wa-taḍaʿuhu ʿalā baʿḍihi
sentences.l: And she said in her-self: Not (is) this-one the cause of its decrease, because she brings it from the hole of the-one-who pilfered-it and puts-it on the rest-of-it.
sentences.i: And she said to herself, “She is not the cause of the loss: she is bringing it back from the hole of whoever stole it and putting it back on the rest.
sentences.n: The print runs mā hādhihi together as ماهذه; the spacing is kept. The mā here is the negative, “this one is not”, not the question “what is this?”. The feminine hādhihi, “this one”, is the weasel, with the masculine noun sabab, “cause”, as its predicate. min juḥri alladhī ikhtalasahu, “from the hole of him who pilfered it”: the woman supposes some other, unknown thief (masculine), whose hole the weasel is robbing. The phrase may also be a loose way of saying min al-juḥri alladhī, “from the hole into which (it was) pilfered”; either way the woman is deceived.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَتْ إِلَيْنَا فِي رَدِّ السِّمْسِمِ وَمَا جَزَاءُ مَنْ أَحْسَنَ إِلَّا أَنْ يُحْسَنَ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad aḥsanat ilaynā fī raddi al-simsimi wa-mā jazāʾu man aḥsana illā an yuḥsana ilayhi
sentences.l: And she has done-good to-us in the returning of the sesame; and what (is) the reward of whoever has-done-good except that good be-done to-him?
sentences.i: She has done us a kindness in bringing the sesame back, and what is the reward of one who does good, but that good be done to her?
sentences.n: aḥsana ilā, “to do good to, be kind to”. The question echoes Qurʾān 55:60, hal jazāʾu al-iḥsāni illā al-iḥsān, “is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?”.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَتْ هَذِهِ آفَةً فِى السِّمْسِمِ وَلَكِنْ لَا أَزَالُ أَرْصُدُهُ حَتَّى يَقَعَ وَأَعْلَمَ مَنْ هُوَ
sentences.tr: wa-laysat hādhihi āfatan fī al-simsimi wa-lākin lā azālu arṣuduhu ḥattā yaqaʿa wa-aʿlama man huwa
sentences.l: And not is this-one a blight in the sesame; but I-will-not cease lying-in-wait-for-him until he falls (into my hands) and I know who he (is).
sentences.i: This one is no plague on the sesame. But I shall keep watching for the thief until he is caught and I know who he is.”
sentences.n: āfa, “a blight, a pest, a bane”. The masculine -hu in arṣuduhu and the verb yaqaʿa point to the imagined thief. waqaʿa, “to fall”, here “to fall into one's hands, be caught”.

sentences.t: فَعَلِمَتْ بِنْتُ عِرْسٍ مَاخَطَرَ بِبَالِ تِلْكَ الْمَرْأَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿalimat bintu ʿirsin mā khaṭara bi-bāli tilka al-marʾati
sentences.l: And the weasel knew what had-occurred to the mind of that woman.
sentences.i: The weasel knew what had passed through the woman's mind.
sentences.n: The print runs mā khaṭara together as ماخطر; the spacing is kept. khaṭara bi-bālihi, “it occurred to him, crossed his mind”: bāl, “mind”, with bi-, “in”.

sentences.t: فَانْطَلَقَتْ إِلَى الْفَأْرَةِ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا أُخْتِي إِنَّهُ لَا خَيْرَ فِيمَنْ لَا يُرَاعِى الْمُجَاوَرَةَ وَلَا يَثْبُتُ عَلَى الْمَوَدَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-inṭalaqat ilā al-faʾrati wa-qālat lahā yā ukhtī innahu lā khayra fī-man lā yurāʿī al-mujāwarata wa-lā yathbutu ʿalā al-mawaddati
sentences.l: And she went-off to the mouse and said to-her: O my-sister, indeed-it-is (that) there-is-no good in-whoever does-not observe the neighbourship and does-not stand-firm upon the affection.
sentences.i: Then she went off to the mouse and said to her, “Sister, there is no good in one who does not honour the bond of neighbours and does not hold fast to friendship.”
sentences.n: yurāʿī, “to observe, have regard for”, is spelt here with ى for final ي, يراعى, as the print often does. al-mujāwara, “neighbourliness, living side by side”. innahu, “indeed it is (the case that)”, the “pronoun of the matter” that introduces a whole clause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْفَأْرَةُ نَعَمْ يَا خَلِيلَتِي وَأَنْعِمْ بِكِ وَبِجِوَارِكِ فَمَا سَبَبُ هَذَا الْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-faʾratu naʿam yā khalīlatī wa-anʿim biki wa-bi-jiwāriki fa-mā sababu hādhā al-kalāmi
sentences.l: And the mouse said: Yes, O my-bosom-friend, and how-blessed (are) you and your-neighbourship! So what (is) the cause of this speech?
sentences.i: The mouse said, “Yes, my dear friend, and what a blessing you are, you and your neighbourliness! But why do you say this?”
sentences.n: naʿam wa-anʿim, “yes, and most gladly”, a stock reply that plays on the root n-ʿ-m. anʿim bi-, the afʿil bi- form of wonder, “how blessed is …!”: the bi- marks the thing admired. khalīla, “a close friend” (fem. of khalīl).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بِنْتُ عِرْسٍ إِنَّ رَبَّ الْبَيْتِ أَتَى بِسِمْسِمٍ فَأَكَلَ مِنْهُ هُوَ وَعِيَالُهُ وَشَبِعُوا وَاسْتَغْنَوْا عَنْهُ وَتَرَكُوهُ كَثِيرًا
sentences.tr: qālat bintu ʿirsin inna rabba al-bayti atā bi-simsimin fa-akala minhu huwa wa-ʿiyāluhu wa-shabiʿū wa-istaghnaw ʿanhu wa-tarakūhu kathīran
sentences.l: The weasel said: Indeed the lord of the house came with sesame, and ate from-it he and his-household, and they-were-sated, and could-do-without it, and left-it plenty.
sentences.i: The weasel said, “The master of the house has brought home some sesame. He and his family have eaten of it till they were full and want no more, and they have left a great deal of it.
sentences.n: rabb al-bayt, “the lord of the house”, the householder. ʿiyāl, “dependants, family”. istaghnā ʿan, “to have no further need of”. kathīran, “(as) plenty”: they left it in abundance. The weasel's story is a lie, told to lure the mouse.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَخَذَ مِنْهُ كُلُّ ذِي رُوحٍ فَلَوْ أَخَذْتِ أَنْتِ الْأُخْرَى كُنْتِ أَحَقَّ بِهِ مِمَّنْ أَخَذَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad akhadha minhu kullu dhī rūḥin fa-law akhadhti anti al-ukhrā kunti aḥaqqa bihi mimman akhadha minhu
sentences.l: And every possessor of a spirit has taken from-it; so if you took, you the-other (too), you-would-be more-entitled to-it than-whoever has-taken from-it.
sentences.i: Every living thing has had some of it; so if you took some too, you would have a better right to it than any of them.”
sentences.n: dhū rūḥ, “possessor of a spirit”, a living creature. anti al-ukhrā, “you, the other one”, colloquial for “you too”. aḥaqqu bi-, “more deserving of”.

sentences.t: فَأَعْجَبَ الْفَأْرَةَ ذَلِكَ وَزَقْزَقَتْ وَرَقَصَتْ وَلَعِبَتْ آذَانُهَا وَذَنَبُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-aʿjaba al-faʾrata dhālika wa-zaqzaqat wa-raqaṣat wa-laʿibat ādhānuhā wa-dhanabuhā
sentences.l: And that pleased the mouse, and she squeaked, and danced, and her ears and her tail played.
sentences.i: The mouse was delighted. She squeaked and danced, and her ears and tail twitched with glee.
sentences.n: aʿjaba, “to please”: the thing that pleases is the subject, here dhālika, and the one pleased is the object, al-faʾrata. zaqzaqa, “to chirp, squeak”, a sound-word.

sentences.t: وَغَرَّهَا الطَّمَعُ فِى السِّمْسِمِ فَقَامَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ بَيْتِهَا فَرَأَتِ السِّمْسِمَ مُجَفَّفًا مَقْشُورًا يَلْمَعُ مِنَ الْبَيَاضِ وَالْمَرْأَةُ جَالِسَةٌ تَرْصُدُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-gharrahā al-ṭamaʿu fī al-simsimi fa-qāmat min waqtihā wa-kharajat min baytihā fa-raʾati al-simsima mujaffafan maqshūran yalmaʿu mina al-bayāḍi wa-al-marʾatu jālisatun tarṣuduhu
sentences.l: And the greed for the sesame deluded-her, and she rose from her-time (at once) and went-out from her house, and she saw the sesame dried, husked, gleaming from the whiteness, and the woman sitting watching-it.
sentences.i: Greed for the sesame led her astray. She got up that very moment and left her hole, and saw the sesame, dried and husked and gleaming white, and the woman sitting there watching it.
sentences.n: gharra, “to beguile, delude”. min waqtihā, “from her moment”, at once. wa-al-marʾatu jālisatun, a circumstantial clause: the woman was sitting there all the while.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تُفَكِّرِ الْفَأْرَةُ فِي عَاقِبَةِ الْأَمْرِ وَكَانَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ قَدِ اسْتَعَدَّتْ بِهِرَاوَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lam tufakkiri al-faʾratu fī ʿāqibati al-amri wa-kānati al-marʾatu qadi istaʿaddat bi-hirāwatin
sentences.l: And the mouse did-not think on the outcome of the matter; and the woman had made-herself-ready with a cudgel.
sentences.i: The mouse gave no thought to how the matter might end; and the woman had armed herself with a club.
sentences.n: istaʿadda bi-, “to get ready, equip oneself with”. hirāwa, “a cudgel, a thick stick”.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تَتَمَالَكِ الْفَأْرَةُ نَفْسَهَا إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَتْ فِى السِّمْسِمِ وَخَالَطَتْهُ وَعَاشَتْ فِيهِ وَصَارَتْ تَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam tatamālaki al-faʾratu nafsahā ilā an dakhalat fī al-simsimi wa-khālaṭathu wa-ʿāshat fīhi wa-ṣārat taʾkulu minhu
sentences.l: And the mouse did-not control herself, until she entered into the sesame, and mingled-with-it, and lived in-it, and began eating from-it.
sentences.i: The mouse could not hold herself back, but went right into the sesame, burrowed about in it, made herself at home there, and set to eating.
sentences.n: lam tatamālak nafsahā, “she could not master herself”. ʿāshat fīhi, “she lived in it”, revelled in it; the word may also be a slip for the similar-looking ʿāthat fīhi, “she made havoc in it”. The print's word is kept. ṣāra with a present verb, “to begin doing”.

sentences.t: فَضَرَبَتْهَا الْمَرْأَةُ بِتِلْكَ الْهِرَاوَةِ فَشَجَّتْ رَأْسَهَا وَكَانَ سَبَبُ هَلَاكِهَا الطَّمَعَ وَغَفْلَتَهَا عَنْ عَوَاقِبِ الْأُمُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍarabathā al-marʾatu bi-tilka al-hirāwati fa-shajjat raʾsahā wa-kāna sababu halākihā al-ṭamaʿa wa-ghaflatahā ʿan ʿawāqibi al-umūri
sentences.l: And the woman struck-her with that cudgel and split her head; and the cause of her perishing was the greed and her heedlessness of the consequences of the affairs.
sentences.i: Then the woman struck her with the club and split her skull open. What destroyed her was greed, and her heedlessness of where things lead.
sentences.n: shajja, “to cleave, break (a head)”. ghafla ʿan, “heedlessness of”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ يَا شَهْرَزَادُ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ هَذِهِ أُحْدُوثَةٌ مَلِيحَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku yā Shahrazādu wa-allāhi inna hādhihi uḥdūthatun malīḥatun
sentences.l: And the king said: O Shahrazād, by-God, indeed this (is) a tale pretty.
sentences.i: The king said, “By God, Shahrazād, that is a fine tale.
sentences.n: The fable ends and the frame breaks in: King Shahriyār speaks. uḥdūtha, “a story, a thing told”, from ḥadatha, “to happen”. malīḥ, “pretty, pleasing”.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ عِنْدَكِ حَدِيثٌ فِي دِمْنِ الصَّدَاقَةِ وَحِفْظِهَا عِنْدَ الشِّدَّةِ فِي التَّخَلُّصِ مِنَ الْهَلَكَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-hal ʿindaki ḥadīthun fī dimni al-ṣadāqati wa-ḥifẓihā ʿinda al-shiddati fī al-takhalluṣi mina al-halakati
sentences.l: So is-there with-you a story on the (?) of friendship, and the keeping-of-it at the hardship, in the escaping from the perdition?
sentences.i: Have you a story about friendship, and keeping faith with a friend in hard times, to escape destruction?”
sentences.n: The word printed دمن is uncertain. It is pointed here as dimn, but no ordinary sense of that word (“dung, the traces of an old camp”) fits. Perhaps it stands for ḍimn, “within, concerning”, which would give “a story concerning friendship”, or for another word such as yumn, “the blessing (of friendship)”. The print's letters are kept and the translation leaves the word out. halaka, “perdition, ruin”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam
sentences.l: She said: Yes.
sentences.i: She said: Yes.

sentences.t: بَلَغَنِي أَنَّ غُرَابًا وَسِنَّوْرًا كَانَا مُتَأَخِّيَيْنِ
sentences.tr: balaghanī anna ghurāban wa-sinnawran kānā mutaʾakhkhiyayni
sentences.l: It-has-reached-me that a crow and a cat were-two having-taken-each-other-as-brothers.
sentences.i: It has reached me that a crow and a cat had sworn brotherhood.
sentences.n: A new fable. sinnawr, “cat”, a literary word; the tale's end calls the same animal by the everyday qiṭṭ. mutaʾakhkhiyayn, dual of mutaʾakhkhī, “having made brotherhood with”, from taʾakhkhā, a derived form of akh, “brother”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا تَحْتَ شَجَرَةٍ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ إِذْرَأَ يَا نَمِرًا مُقْبِلًا عَلَى تِلْكَ الشَّجَرَةِ الَّتِي كَانَا تَحْتَهَا وَلَمْ يَعْلَمَا بِهِ حَتَّى صَارَ قَرِيبًا مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā taḥta shajaratin ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati idh raʾayā namiran muqbilan ʿalā tilka al-shajarati allatī kānā taḥtahā wa-lam yaʿlamā bihi ḥattā ṣāra qarīban mina al-shajarati
sentences.l: And while they-two (were) under a tree in that state, behold, they-two-saw a leopard advancing towards that tree which they-two were under-it, and they-two-did-not know of-him until he had-become near to the tree.
sentences.i: Once, while the two of them were sitting thus under a tree, they suddenly saw a leopard making for the very tree they were under; and they did not notice him until he was close to it.
sentences.n: The print splits the words wrongly as اذرأ يا; they are idh raʾayā, “when (suddenly) the two saw”, and the print's spacing is kept. baynamā … idh, “while … suddenly”. namir is the leopard (or panther), not the tiger. muqbil ʿalā, “coming towards”.

sentences.t: فَطَارَ الْغُرَابُ إِلَى أَعْلَى الشَّجَرَةِ وَبَقِيَ السِّنَّوْرُ مُتَحَيِّرًا
sentences.tr: fa-ṭāra al-ghurābu ilā aʿlā al-shajarati wa-baqiya al-sinnawru mutaḥayyiran
sentences.l: And the crow flew to the top of the tree, and the cat remained bewildered.
sentences.i: The crow flew up to the top of the tree, and the cat was left at a loss.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِلْغُرَابِ يَاخَلِيلِي هَلْ عِنْدَكَ حِيلَةٌ فِي خَلَاصِي كَمَا هُوَ الرَّجَاءُ فِيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-al-ghurābi yā khalīlī hal ʿindaka ḥīlatun fī khalāṣī kamā huwa al-rajāʾu fīka
sentences.l: And he said to the crow: O my-bosom-friend, is-there with-you a stratagem for my-deliverance, as is the hope in-you?
sentences.i: He said to the crow, “My friend, have you some trick to save me, as I hope you have?”
sentences.n: The print runs yā khalīlī together as ياخليلي; the spacing is kept. ḥīla, “a device, a stratagem”, the key word of this fable. al-rajāʾu fīka, “the hope (placed) in you”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْغُرَابُ إِنَّمَا تُلْتَمَسُ الْإِخْوَانُ عِنْدَ الْحَاجَةِ إِلَيْهِمْ فِى الْحِيلَةِ عِنْدَ نُزُولِ الْمَكْرُوهِ بِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ghurābu innamā tultamasu al-ikhwānu ʿinda al-ḥājati ilayhim fī al-ḥīlati ʿinda nuzūli al-makrūhi bihim
sentences.l: And the crow said to-him: Only are-sought the brothers at the need for-them in the stratagem, at the descending of the hateful upon-them.
sentences.i: The crow answered, “It is for just such times that brothers are sought out: when one needs their cunning, when misfortune falls on them.
sentences.n: innamā, “only, it is precisely”. iltamasa, “to seek”, here in the passive with the broken plural al-ikhwān treated as feminine. al-makrūh, “the hateful thing”, a misfortune. The last bihim, “upon them”, is loose: it means upon those who seek help.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aḥsana qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And how fair (is) the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: How well the poet put it:
sentences.n: mā aḥsana, “how fine is …!”, the verb of wonder, with its object in the accusative.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ صَدِيْقَ الْحَقِّ مَنْ كَانَ مَعَكْ * وَمَنْ يَضُرُّ نَفْسَهُ لِيَنْفَعَكْ
وَمَنْ اِذَا رَيْبُ الزَّمَانِ صَدَّعَكَ * شَتَّتَ فِيكَ نَفْسَهُ لِيَجْمَعَكَ
sentences.tr:
inna ṣadīqa al-ḥaqqi man kāna maʿak * wa-man yaḍurru nafsahu li-yanfaʿak
wa-man idhā raybu al-zamāni ṣaddaʿaka * shattata fīka nafsahu li-yajmaʿaka
sentences.l:
Indeed the friend of the truth (is) whoever was with-you, * and whoever harms his-self so-that he-may-benefit-you;
and whoever, when the doubtful-chance of the time has-split-you, * scatters for-you his-self so-that he-may-gather-you.
sentences.i:
Your true friend is the one who stands by you, * who will harm himself to do you good;
who, when the blows of fortune break you apart, * spends himself freely to make you whole.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. ṣadīq al-ḥaqq, “the friend of truth”, a true friend. rayb al-zamān, “the vicissitude of time”, the blows of fortune. ṣaddaʿa, “to crack, split”; shattata, “to scatter, disperse”, set against jamaʿa, “to gather”: the friend breaks himself in pieces to put you back together. The first line rhymes in -ʿak, the second in -ʿaka with the vowel sounded.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ قَرِيبًا مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ رُعَاةٌ مَعَهُمْ كِلَابٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna qarīban mina al-shajarati ruʿātun maʿahum kilābun
sentences.l: And there-was near to the tree herdsmen, with-them dogs.
sentences.i: Now near the tree there were some herdsmen who had dogs with them.
sentences.n: The damma in رُعاة is the print's own. kāna stands in the singular before its plural subject ruʿāt, “herdsmen”, as the verb regularly does when it comes first.

sentences.t: فَذَهَبَ الْغُرَابُ حَتَّى ضَرَبَ بِجَنَاحِهِ وَجْهَ الْأَرْضِ وَنَعَقَ وَصَاحَ
sentences.tr: fa-dhahaba al-ghurābu ḥattā ḍaraba bi-janāḥihi wajha al-arḍi wa-naʿaqa wa-ṣāḥa
sentences.l: And the crow went until he struck with his wing the face of the ground, and croaked, and cried-out.
sentences.i: The crow flew off until he was beating the ground with his wing, cawing and crying out.
sentences.n: naʿaqa, “to croak, caw”, the crow's own cry.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَضَرَبَ بِجَنَاحِهِ وَجْهَ بَعْضِ الْكِلَابِ وَارْتَفَعَ قَلِيلًا وَتَبِعَتْهُ الْكِلَابُ وَصَارَتْ فِي أَثَرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama ilayhim wa-ḍaraba bi-janāḥihi wajha baʿḍi al-kilābi wa-irtafaʿa qalīlan wa-tabiʿathu al-kilābu wa-ṣārat fī atharihi
sentences.l: Then he advanced to-them and struck with his wing the face of one of the dogs, and rose a-little, and the dogs followed-him and came-to-be in his track.
sentences.i: Then he went up to them, struck one of the dogs in the face with his wing, and rose a little way; and the dogs went after him, hard on his track.
sentences.n: fī atharihi, “in his trace”, close behind him.

sentences.t: فَرَفَعَ الرَّاعِي رَأْسَهُ فَرَأَى طَائِرًا يَطِيرُ قَرِيبًا مِنَ الْأَرْضِ وَيَقَعُ فَتَبِعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-rafaʿa al-rāʿī raʾsahu fa-raʾā ṭāʾiran yaṭīru qarīban mina al-arḍi wa-yaqaʿu fa-tabiʿahu
sentences.l: And the herdsman raised his head and saw a bird flying near to the ground and alighting, and he followed-it.
sentences.i: The herdsman looked up and saw a bird flying low over the ground and settling, and he followed it.
sentences.n: waqaʿa, “to fall”, of a bird “to alight”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ الْغُرَابُ لَايَطِيرُ إِلَّا بِقَدْرِ النَّجَاةِ وَالْخَلَاصِ مِنَ الْكِلَابِ وَيُطْمِعُهَا فِي أَنْ تَفْتَرِسَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra al-ghurābu lā yaṭīru illā bi-qadri al-najāti wa-al-khalāṣi mina al-kilābi wa-yuṭmiʿuhā fī an taftarisahu
sentences.l: And the crow came-to not fly except by the measure of the escape and the getting-free from the dogs, and he-made-them-covet that they-might-seize-him.
sentences.i: And the crow flew only just high enough to keep clear of the dogs, tempting them with the hope of catching him.
sentences.n: The print runs lā yaṭīru together as لايطير; the spacing is kept. bi-qadri, “by the measure of”, just enough for. aṭmaʿa fī, “to make (someone) covet, raise hopes of”. iftarasa, “to seize and tear prey”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ ارْتَفَعَ قَلِيلًا وَتَبِعَتْهُ الْكِلَابُ حَتَّى انْتَهَى إِلَى الشَّجَرَةِ الَّتِي تَحْتَهَا النَّمِرُ
sentences.tr: thumma irtafaʿa qalīlan wa-tabiʿathu al-kilābu ḥattā intahā ilā al-shajarati allatī taḥtahā al-namiru
sentences.l: Then he rose a-little, and the dogs followed-him, until he reached the tree which under-it (was) the leopard.
sentences.i: Then he rose a little higher, with the dogs following, until he came to the tree where the leopard was.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الْكِلَابُ النَّمِرَ وَثَبَتْ عَلَيْهِ فَوَلَّى هَارِبًا وَكَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ يَأْكُلُ الْقِطَّ فَنَجَى مِنْهُ ذَلِكَ الْقِطُّ بِحِيلَةِ صَاحِبِهِ الْغُرَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-kilābu al-namira wathabat ʿalayhi fa-wallā hāriban wa-kāna yaẓunnu annahu yaʾkulu al-qiṭṭa fa-najā minhu dhālika al-qiṭṭu bi-ḥīlati ṣāḥibihi al-ghurābi
sentences.l: And when the dogs saw the leopard they leapt upon-him, and he turned-away fleeing; and he had been thinking that he would-eat the cat. And that cat escaped from-him by the stratagem of his companion the crow.
sentences.i: When the dogs saw the leopard they sprang at him, and he turned and fled, though he had thought to eat the cat. So the cat escaped him through the cunning of his friend the crow.
sentences.n: The sukūn in وثبتْ is the print's own. wallā hāriban, “he turned his back, fleeing”. The print spells najā, “he escaped”, with ى, فنجى, where Classical spelling has ا (the root is n-j-w); the spelling is kept. The cat, sinnawr at the start, is here the everyday qiṭṭ.

sentences.t: فَهَذِهِ الْحِكَايَةُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ تَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ مَوَدَّةَ إِخْوَانِ الصَّفَا تُخَلِّصُ وَتُنْجِي مِنَ الْهَلَكَاتِ وَالْوُقُوعِ فِى الْمَعَاطِبِ
sentences.tr: fa-hādhihi al-ḥikāyatu ayyuhā al-maliku tadullu ʿalā anna mawaddata ikhwāni al-ṣafā tukhalliṣu wa-tunjī mina al-halakāti wa-al-wuqūʿi fī al-maʿāṭibi
sentences.l: And this tale, O king, points to (the fact) that the affection of the brothers of purity delivers and saves from the perditions and the falling into the places-of-ruin.
sentences.i: This tale, O king, shows that the love of true and faithful friends delivers a man and saves him from destruction and from falling into ruin.
sentences.n: The print has فهده, a misprint for فهذه, corrected here. ikhwān al-ṣafā, “brothers of purity”, friends whose loyalty is clear of self-interest; the phrase is also the name of a tenth-century brotherhood of philosophers, who themselves drew on these animal fables. maʿāṭib, plural of maʿṭab, “a place of ruin, a peril”.

sentences.t: وَحُكِيَ أَنَّ ثَعْلَبًا سَكَنَ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنَ الْجَبَلِ وَكَانَ كُلَّمَا وَلَدَ وَلَدًا وَاشْتَدَّ وَلَدُهُ أَكَلَهُ مِنَ الْجُوعِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥukiya anna thaʿlaban sakana fī baytin mina al-jabali wa-kāna kullamā walada waladan wa-ishtadda waladuhu akalahu mina al-jūʿi
sentences.l: And it-was-told that a fox dwelt in a house (= den) of the mountain, and it-was (that) whenever he bore a young-one and his young-one grew-strong, he-ate-it from the hunger.
sentences.i: It is told that a fox lived in a den in the mountain, and whenever he had a cub and the cub grew sturdy, he would eat it out of hunger.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, of the fox and the crow. ḥukiya, “it has been told”, passive of ḥakā, a stock opener for a story. bayt, “house”, is here the fox's lair. walada, “to give birth”, is used of the fox, who is grammatically masculine throughout: the Arabic thinks of the species, not the sex. ishtadda, “to become strong”, here “to grow big enough to be worth eating”.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ لَمْ يَأْكُلْ وَلَدَهُ وَخَلَّاهُ وَيَقْعُدْ عِنْدَهُ وَيَحْفَظْهُ وَيَحْرُسْهُ مَاتَ مِنَ الْجُوعِ وَأَضَرَّبِهِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-in lam yaʾkul waladahu wa-khallāhu wa-yaqʿud ʿindahu wa-yaḥfaẓhu wa-yaḥrus-hu māta mina al-jūʿi wa-aḍarra bihi dhālika
sentences.l: And if he did-not eat his young-one, and left-it-alone, and sat by-it and kept-it and guarded-it, he-died from the hunger; and that harmed him.
sentences.i: But if he did not eat his cub, and spared it and sat by it to watch over it and guard it, he was dying of hunger; and this did him great harm.
sentences.n: The sentence runs on loosely, as the text often does: after lam yaʾkul, “did not eat”, the print switches to a perfect, khallāhu, “he let it be”, then back to imperfects, which are pointed here as still governed by lam. māta, “he died”, is meant as “he was like to die”, since the fox lives on. واضربه is the print's run-together spelling of wa-aḍarra bihi, “and it harmed him”, set as one word; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يَأْوِي إِلَى ذِرْوَةِ ذَلِكَ الْجَبَلِ غُرَابٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yaʾwī ilā dhirwati dhālika al-jabali ghurābun
sentences.l: And there-was (one who) used-to-resort to the summit of that mountain: a crow.
sentences.i: Now a crow used to roost on the summit of that mountain.
sentences.n: The subject, ghurābun, “a crow”, comes last, after its verb and the place: the sentence keeps the crow back for its final word. awā ilā, “to take shelter in, to make one's home at”; dhirwa, “top, peak”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ فِي نَفْسِهِ أُرِيدُأَنْ أَعْقِدَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ هَذَا الْغُرَابِ مَوَدَّةً وَأَجْعَلَهُ لِي مُؤْنِسًا عَلَى الْوَحْدَةِ مُعَاوِنًا عَلَى طَلَبِ الرِّزْقِ لِأَنَّهُ يَقْدِرُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَالَا أَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-thaʿlabu fī nafsihi urīdu an aʿqida baynī wa-bayna hādhā al-ghurābi mawaddatan wa-ajʿalahu lī muʾnisan ʿalā al-waḥdati muʿāwinan ʿalā ṭalabi al-rizqi li-annahu yaqdiru min dhālika ʿalā mā lā aqdiru ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And the fox said in his-soul: I-want to tie between-me and-between this crow an affection, and make-him for-me a companion against the solitude, a helper in the seeking of the provision, because he is-able of that to what I-am-not able to.
sentences.i: The fox said to himself, “I should like to bind this crow to me in friendship, and make him my companion in my loneliness and my helper in seeking food; for in that he can do what I cannot.”
sentences.n: fī nafsihi, “in his soul”: to himself. اريدان is the print's spacing for urīdu an, “I want to”, and مالا for mā lā, “what … not”; both are kept as set. ʿaqada mawaddatan, “to tie a bond of affection”. rizq, “provision, daily bread”, what God allots each creature to live on.

sentences.t: فَدَنَا الثَّعْلَبُ مِنَ الْغُرَابِ حَتَّى صَارَ قَرِيبًا مِنْهُ بِحَيْثُ يَسْمَعُ كَلَامَهُ فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-danā al-thaʿlabu mina al-ghurābi ḥattā ṣāra qarīban minhu bi-ḥaythu yasmaʿu kalāmahu fa-sallama ʿalayhi
sentences.l: So the fox drew-near to the crow until he became near to-him, so-that he-could-hear his speech, and he-greeted him.
sentences.i: So the fox drew near the crow until he was close enough for the crow to hear him, and greeted him.
sentences.n: bi-ḥaythu, “in such a way that”, gives the degree: near enough to be heard. sallama ʿalā, “to say peace to”, to greet with al-salāmu ʿalaykum.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ يَاجَارِي إِنَّ لِلْجَارِ الْمُسْلِمِ عَلَى الْجَارِ الْمُسْلِمِ حَقَّيْنِ حَقَّ الْجِيرَةِ وَحَقَّ الْإِسْلَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu yā jārī inna li-al-jāri al-muslimi ʿalā al-jāri al-muslimi ḥaqqayni ḥaqqa al-jīrati wa-ḥaqqa al-islāmi
sentences.l: Then he-said to-him: O my-neighbour, indeed to the Muslim neighbour upon the Muslim neighbour (belong) two-rights: the right of the neighbourhood and the right of the Islam.
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Neighbour, a Muslim neighbour has two claims on a Muslim neighbour: the claim of neighbourliness and the claim of Islam.
sentences.n: ياجاري is set as one word, yā jārī, “O my neighbour”; the spacing is kept. li- … ʿalā, “belonging to … binding on”, is the usual way of stating a right one party holds over another. ḥaqqa … wa-ḥaqqa stand in apposition to ḥaqqayni, explaining the two. The animals of the fable speak as Muslims, a stock touch of the genre.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ يَا خَلِيلِي بِأَنَّكَ جَارِي وَلَكَ عَلَيَّ حَقٌّ يَجِبُ قَضَاؤُهُ وَخُصُوصًا مَعَ طُولِ الْمُجَاوَرَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam yā khalīlī bi-annaka jārī wa-laka ʿalayya ḥaqqun yajibu qaḍāʾuhu wa-khuṣūṣan maʿa ṭūli al-mujāwarati
sentences.l: And know, O my-friend, that you (are) my-neighbour, and to-you upon-me (is) a right whose discharging is-binding, and especially with the length of the neighbouring.
sentences.i: Know, my friend, that you are my neighbour, and have a claim on me that I am bound to honour, all the more since we have lived side by side so long.
sentences.n: khalīl, “close friend, intimate”. iʿlam bi-anna, “know that”: the bi- is a common, optional addition after verbs of knowing. qaḍāʾ here is “paying off, discharging” a debt or duty.

sentences.t: عَلَى أَنَّ فِي صَدْرِي وَدِيعَةً مِنْ مَحَبَّتِكَ دَعَتْنِي إِلَى مُلَاطَفَتِكَ وَبَعَثَتْنِي عَلَى الْتِمَاسِ أُخُوَّتِكَ فَمَا عِنْدَكَ مِنَ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: ʿalā anna fī ṣadrī wadīʿatan min maḥabbatika daʿatnī ilā mulāṭafatika wa-baʿathatnī ʿalā iltimāsi ukhuwwatika fa-mā ʿindaka mina al-jawābi
sentences.l: Besides that in my-breast (is) a deposit of love-of-you; it-called-me to treating-you-kindly and it-roused-me to seeking your brotherhood. So what (is) with-you of the answer?
sentences.i: Besides, there lies in my breast a store of love for you, which has moved me to show you kindness and urged me to ask for your brotherhood. So what answer have you?”
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, corrected here. ʿalā anna, “moreover, besides the fact that”. wadīʿa, “a thing deposited in trust”: the love is pictured as something placed in his keeping. baʿatha ʿalā, “to drive, incite to”. iltimās, “seeking, requesting”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْغُرَابُ لِلثَّعْلَبِ إِنَّ خَيْرَ الْقَوْلِ أَصْدَقُهُ وَرُبَّمَا تَتَحَدَّثُ بِلِسَانِكَ مَالَيْسَ فِي قَلْبِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ghurābu li-al-thaʿlabi inna khayra al-qawli aṣdaquhu wa-rubbamā tataḥaddathu bi-lisānika mā laysa fī qalbika
sentences.l: And the crow said to-him, to the fox: Indeed the best of the speech (is) its-truest, and perhaps you-speak with your-tongue what is-not in your-heart.
sentences.i: The crow answered the fox, “The best speech is the truest. It may be that you say with your tongue what is not in your heart;
sentences.n: lahu … li-al-thaʿlabi, “to him … to the fox”, names the hearer twice: a pleonasm common in this text, kept as printed. The marks in وربّما and تتحدّث are the print's own. ماليس, set as one word, is mā laysa, “what is not”. khayru al-qawli aṣdaquhu, “the best of speech is its truest”, has the ring of a proverb.

sentences.t: وَأَخْشَى أَنْ تَكُونَ أُخُوَّتُكَ بِاللِّسَانِ ظَاهِرًا وَعَدَاوَتُكَ فِى الْقَلْبِ بَاطِنًا لِأَنَّكَ آكِلٌ وَأَنَا مَأْكُولٌ فَوَجَبَ لَنَا التَّبَايُنُ فِى الْمَحَبَّةِ وَالْمُوَاصَلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhshā an takūna ukhuwwatuka bi-al-lisāni ẓāhiran wa-ʿadāwatuka fī al-qalbi bāṭinan li-annaka ākilun wa-anā maʾkūlun fa-wajaba lanā al-tabāyunu fī al-maḥabbati wa-al-muwāṣalati
sentences.l: And I-fear that your brotherhood should-be with the tongue outwardly and your enmity in the heart inwardly, because you (are) an-eater and I (am) eaten; so there-is-binding for-us the being-apart in the love and the keeping-company.
sentences.i: and I fear your brotherhood may be on your tongue, outwardly, and your enmity in your heart, within. For you are the eater and I am the eaten, and so we are bound to stay apart in love and in company.
sentences.n: ẓāhiran … bāṭinan, “outwardly … inwardly”, are adverbial accusatives, hence masculine though they follow feminine nouns; the pair is a rhyming contrast. ākil … maʾkūl, active and passive participles of the same root: “eater … eaten”. tabāyun, “mutual distance, being at odds”.

sentences.t: فَمَا الَّذِى دَعَاكَ إِلَى طَلَبِ مَالَاتُدْرِكُ وَإِرَادَةِ مَالَا يَكُونُ وَأَنْتَ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْوَحْشِ وَأَنَا مِنْ جِنْسِ الطَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā alladhī daʿāka ilā ṭalabi mā lā tudriku wa-irādati mā lā yakūnu wa-anta min jinsi al-waḥshi wa-anā min jinsi al-ṭayri
sentences.l: So what (is) that-which called-you to the seeking of what you-do-not attain and the wanting of what will-not be, while you (are) of the kind of the wild-beasts and I (am) of the kind of the birds?
sentences.i: What has led you to seek what you cannot reach and want what can never be, when you are of the race of beasts and I of the race of birds?
sentences.n: مالاتدرك and مالا are the print's spacing for mā lā tudriku and mā lā; kept as set. wa-anta …, “while you …”, a circumstantial clause. waḥsh, “wild animals”, as against the tame.

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ الْأُخُوَّةُ لَا تَتِمُّ وَلَاتَصِحُّ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi al-ukhuwwatu lā tatimmu wa-lā taṣiḥḥu
sentences.l: And this brotherhood does-not become-complete and does-not hold-sound.
sentences.i: Such a brotherhood can never be whole or true.”
sentences.n: ولاتصح is set as one word, wa-lā taṣiḥḥu, “and is not sound”. ṣaḥḥa, “to be healthy, valid, genuine”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الثَّعْلَبُ إِنَّ مَنْ عَلِمَ مَوْضِعَ الْأَجِلَّاءِ فَأَحْسَنَ الِاخْتِيَارَ فِيمَا يَخْتَارُهُ مِنْهَا رُبَّمَا يَصِلُ إِلَى مَنَافِعِ الْإِخْوَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-thaʿlabu inna man ʿalima mawḍiʿa al-ajillāʾi fa-aḥsana al-ikhtiyāra fīmā yakhtāruhu minhā rubbamā yaṣilu ilā manāfiʿi al-ikhwāni
sentences.l: And the fox said to-him: Indeed whoever knows the place of the noble-ones and does-well the choosing in what he-chooses of-them, perhaps he-reaches to the benefits of the brothers.
sentences.i: The fox replied, “He who knows where worthy friends are to be found, and chooses well among them, may well come to enjoy the benefits of brotherhood.
sentences.n: The reading of الاجلاء is uncertain. As printed it is most likely al-ajillāʾ, “the eminent, the worthy”, and is pointed so here; but the sense invites al-akhillāʾ, “close friends” (الاخلاء, one dot different), which would fit the talk of brotherhood better. The print is kept. minhā, “of them”, uses the feminine singular for a plural of persons, as Arabic may. rubbamā, “perhaps, it may be”, softens the claim.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَحْبَبْتُ قُرْبَكَ وَاخْتَرْتُ الْأُنْسَ بِكَ لِيَكُونَ بَعْضُنَا عَوْنًا لِبَعْضٍ عَلَى أَغْرَاضِنَا وَتُعْقِبَ مَوَدَّتُنَا نَجَاحًا
sentences.tr: wa-qad aḥbabtu qurbaka wa-ikhtartu al-unsa bika li-yakūna baʿḍunā ʿawnan li-baʿḍin ʿalā aghrāḍinā wa-tuʿqiba mawaddatunā najāḥan
sentences.l: And I-have loved nearness-to-you and chosen the companionship with-you, so-that some-of-us may-be a help to others in our aims, and our affection may-bring-after-it success.
sentences.i: I have come to love your nearness and chosen your company, so that each of us may help the other to his ends, and our friendship may bear fruit in success.
sentences.n: baʿḍunā … li-baʿḍin, “some of us … to some”: the Arabic way of saying “one another”. aʿqaba, “to leave behind as a result, to bring in its train”. aghrāḍ (sing. gharaḍ), “aims, purposes”.

sentences.t: وَعِنْدِى حِكَايَاتٌ فِي حُسْنِ الصَّدَاقَةِ إِنْ أَرَدْتَ أَنْ أَحْكِيَهَا حَكَيْتُهَا لَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿindī ḥikāyātun fī ḥusni al-ṣadāqati in aradta an aḥkiyahā ḥakaytuhā laka
sentences.l: And with-me (are) tales about the goodness of the friendship; if you-wish that I-tell-them, I-tell-them to-you.
sentences.i: I know tales of the worth of friendship, and if you wish to hear them, I will tell them to you.”
sentences.n: ḥakaytuhā, a perfect in the answer of a condition, is future in meaning: “I will tell them”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْغُرَابُ قَدْ أَذِنْتُ لَكَ فِي أَنْ تَبُثَّهَا فَقُلْ وَحَدِّثْنِى بِهَا حَتَّي أَسْمَعَهَا وَأَعِيَهَا وَأَعْرِفَ الْمُرَادَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ghurābu qad adhintu laka fī an tabuththahā fa-qul wa-ḥaddithnī bihā ḥattā asmaʿahā wa-aʿiyahā wa-aʿrifa al-murāda minhā
sentences.l: And the crow said: I-have permitted to-you that you-spread-them; so speak, and relate-to-me of-them, so-that I-hear-them and retain-them and know the meant (sense) from-them.
sentences.i: The crow said, “I give you leave to set them out. Speak, then, and tell them to me, so that I may hear them and keep them in mind and grasp their meaning.”
sentences.n: The shadda in تبثّها is the print's own; bathth is “to spread abroad, to pour out” news or grief. The print spells ḥattā with final ي, حتي, a habit of the text; it is read ḥattā. waʿā, “to hold, to take in and remember”; aʿiyahā is its subjunctive with the pronoun.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الثَّعْلَبُ اسْمَعْ يَا خَلِيلِي يُحْكَى عَنْ بُرْغُوثٍ وَفَأْرَةٍ مَا يُسْتَدَلُّ بِهِ عَلَى مَا ذَكَرْتُهُ لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-thaʿlabu ismaʿ yā khalīlī yuḥkā ʿan burghūthin wa-faʾratin mā yustadallu bihi ʿalā mā dhakartuhu laka
sentences.l: And the fox said to-him: Hear, O my-friend: there-is-told about a flea and a mouse what is-taken-as-proof by-it of what I-mentioned to-you.
sentences.i: The fox said, “Listen, my friend. A story is told of a flea and a mouse that shows the truth of what I have said to you.”
sentences.n: The fable within the fable begins. burghūth, “flea”. istadalla bi- … ʿalā, “to take something as evidence for”; here passive, “by which one is guided to”. The shadda in يستدلّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْغُرَابُ وَكَيْفَ كَانَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ghurābu wa-kayfa kāna dhālika
sentences.l: And the crow said: And how was that?
sentences.i: “And how was that?” asked the crow.
sentences.n: The listener's stock question, which in the Nights brings on a story.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ زَعَمُوا أَنَّ فَارَةً كَانَتْ فِي بَيْتِ رَجُلٍ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ عَظِيمِ التِّجَارَةِ كَثِيرِ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-thaʿlabu zaʿamū anna fāratan kānat fī bayti rajulin mina al-tujjāri ʿaẓīmi al-tijārati kathīri al-māli
sentences.l: And the fox said: They-claimed that a mouse was in the house of a man of the merchants, great of the trade, abundant of the wealth.
sentences.i: The fox said, “They say that a mouse lived in the house of a merchant, a man of great trade and much wealth.
sentences.n: zaʿamū, “they claimed, they say”, is set on a line of its own in the print as the opening of the tale; here it begins the fox's story. The print spells the word for mouse here fāra, without hamza, فارة, though elsewhere in the tale it has فأرة; the softened form is the colloquial one and is kept. ʿaẓīmi al-tijārati, kathīri al-māli, “great of trade, much of wealth”: adjectives in construct, describing the man.

sentences.t: فَأَوَى الْبُرْغُوثُ لَيْلَةً إِلَى فِرَاشِ ذَلِكَ التَّاجِرِ فَوَجَدَ لَهُ بَدَنًا نَاعِمًا
sentences.tr: fa-awā al-burghūthu laylatan ilā firāshi dhālika al-tājiri fa-wajada lahu badanan nāʿiman
sentences.l: And the flea resorted one-night to the bed of that merchant, and found for-him a body soft.
sentences.i: One night the flea made its way into that merchant's bed, and found his body soft and tender.
sentences.n: The flea enters with the article, al-burghūth, as though already known: it is the flea just named. laylatan, “one night”, an adverbial accusative of time. wajada lahu badanan, “he found him to have a body”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْبُرْغُوثُ عَطْشَانًا فَشَرِبَ مِنْ دَمِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-burghūthu ʿaṭshānan fa-shariba min damihi
sentences.l: And the flea was thirsty, so he-drank of his-blood.
sentences.i: The flea was thirsty, and drank of his blood.
sentences.n: ʿaṭshānan takes tanwīn here, as the print's spelling with final alif shows; Classical grammar makes ʿaṭshān a diptote, ʿaṭshāna, without it. The form is the text's own.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ التَّاجِرُ مِنَ الْبُرْغُوثِ أَلَمًا فَاسْتَيْقَظَ مِنَ النَّوْمِ فَجَلَسَ قَاعِدًا وَنَادَى لِجَوَارِيهِ وَبَعْضِ أَتْبَاعِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada al-tājiru mina al-burghūthi alaman fa-istayqaẓa mina al-nawmi fa-jalasa qāʿidan wa-nādā li-jawārīhi wa-baʿḍi atbāʿihi
sentences.l: And the merchant found from the flea a pain, so he-woke from the sleep and sat-up sitting, and called to his slave-girls and some of his followers.
sentences.i: The merchant felt the bite of the flea, woke from his sleep and sat up, and called his slave-girls and some of his servants.
sentences.n: jalasa qāʿidan, “he sat up, sitting”, a pleonasm for emphasis. nādā li-, “to call to”, where Classical prose has nādā with a direct object. jawārī (sing. jāriya), “slave-girls, maidservants”.

sentences.t: فَأَسْرَعُوا إِلَيْهِ وَشَمَّرُوا عَنْ أَيْدِيهِمْ يَطُوفُونَ عَلَى الْبُرْغُوثِ
sentences.tr: fa-asraʿū ilayhi wa-shammarū ʿan aydīhim yaṭūfūna ʿalā al-burghūthi
sentences.l: And they-hastened to-him and tucked-up from their hands (= bared their arms), going-round after the flea.
sentences.i: They hurried to him, rolled back their sleeves, and went hunting all about for the flea.
sentences.n: shammara ʿan, “to tuck up (the garment) off”: to bare the arms for work; the shadda in وشمّروا is the print's own. yaṭūfūna, “going round”, a circumstantial imperfect: they went about searching.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَحَسَّ الْبُرْغُوثُ بِالطَّلَبِ وَلَّى هَارِبًا فَصَادَفَ جُحْرَ الْفَأْرَةِ فَدَخَلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aḥassa al-burghūthu bi-al-ṭalabi wallā hāriban fa-ṣādafa juḥra al-faʾrati fa-dakhalahu
sentences.l: And when the flea sensed the search, he-turned-away fleeing, and came-upon the hole of the mouse and entered-it.
sentences.i: When the flea sensed the hunt, it turned and fled, chanced on the mouse's hole and slipped inside.
